targetReport.title: Statistics Act (Act No. 53 of 2007) — 統計法
targetReport.publisher: National Diet of Japan / Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications (MIC)
targetReport.description: Foundational statute that comprehensively reformed Japan’s official statistics system. Defines official statistics as information infrastructure, establishes fundamental statistics (基幹統計) and fundamental statistical surveys, creates the Statistics Commission, requires a Master Plan concerning the Development of Official Statistics, and sets rules for statistical surveys, confidentiality, secondary use, and coordination across the highly decentralised Japanese statistical system. Replaced the 1947 Statistics Act.
targetReport._notes:
Prime static + recurring-citation node — direct analogue of Mexico’s LSNIEG and Argentina’s Ley 17.622.

Article 1 states the purpose: ‘to promote systematic and efficient development of official statistics and to ensure the usefulness thereof through specifying basic matters concerning the production and provision of official statistics, and thereby to contribute to sound development of the national economy and enhancement of the living standards of the citizens.’

Official statistics are explicitly recognised as ‘information infrastructure’ usable not only by administration but by society as a whole. Fundamental statistics include the Population Census statistics, National Accounts, and other statistics designated by the Minister of Internal Affairs and Communications. Every subsequent methodological document, survey approval, and quality report cites the 2007 Act as the legal foundation. No independent publication cadence is required; continuous institutional citation satisfies the expanded node definition.

results.auditNotes: IMDB record 2318 Estimation text verbatim: IPPI weights derived from 2019 Supply and Use Tables.
results.basis: The reverse direction, and the graph's second mutual pair. Record 2318, under Estimation: 'For the IPPI, commodity and industry weights are derived from a combination of the 2019 Supply and Use Tables that closely reflect actual economic transactions by industry and the sales of goods manufactured by companies as reported for the 2019 ASML.' The same section adds that the industry indexes are 'aggregated to the level required for the input-output tables and the measurement of Gross Domestic Product', so the tables set the aggregation structure as well as the weights. Admissible under the V0.10 mutual-partner rule on its own terms: each direction is stated by a different document in its own words, each carries its own evidence_url, and the two are asymmetric in kind rather than restatements of one relationship — the tables take the IPPI as a price measure, the IPPI takes the tables as a weighting frame. `relationship_type` records the asymmetry as the rule requires: `methodology_depends_on` outbound from the tables against `uses_data_from` here, because the SUT figures are a direct numerical input to the weights rather than a method the IPPI follows. THE MECHANISM IS NOT SIMULTANEOUS AND THAT MATTERS FOR READING THE CYCLE: the 2019 tables weight today's index, and today's index deflates a later vintage of the tables. Nothing circular happens in any single calculation; the loop closes only across vintages, five years apart.

targetReport.title: Supply, Use and Input-Output Tables
targetReport.description: The annual benchmark of the Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts. The supply and use tables trace the production of products by domestic industries, combined with imports, through their use as intermediate inputs or as final consumption, investment or exports, and yield gross value added by industry; the symmetric industry-by-industry input-output tables are derived from them. Record 1401's own description states the tables 'can be used to calculate economy-wide gross domestic product (GDP) either directly, by summing value added over the industries, or indirectly, by summing to the economy-wide cost of primary inputs (income-based GDP) or by computing the grand total of the flow of products into final use categories (expenditure-based GDP) - the link to the national income and expenditure accounts.' Both the monthly GDP by industry programme and the quarterly income and expenditure accounts are projections off this benchmark, which is the actual shape of the Canadian accounts and was not representable in this graph until now.
targetReport.cadence_note: Annual, reference period calendar year, but with an unusually long lag: record 1401 states the tables 'are available about two and half years after the end of the reference year; this is because of the delay in obtaining the needed source data and by the complex nature of producing such a detailed account.' The programme also releases derived products on separate dates — the 2026 release schedule lists April 15 for the input-output tables, May 4 for value added in exports and June 16 for the economic impact of wireless telecommunications carriers — so releases_per_year 1 counts the benchmark tables and not the satellite products.

Kenya implemented e-GDDS (with a National Summary Data Page) around 2018, per the IMF's own DSBB e-GDDS pages and confirmed via a related IMF press release. A notch below South Africa and Egypt, both confirmed on full SDDS -- worth having as a distinct node so the graph can actually show the tiering rather than treating every country's IMF dissemination status as equivalent.

targetReport.title: Estadísticas de Comercio Exterior / Merchandise Trade
targetReport.description: Monthly and annual statistics of exports and imports of goods, with a sharp analytical split between oil and non-oil trade.
targetReport._notes: Trade data feed the BOP and national accounts. Non-oil exports (shrimp, cocoa, banana, mining) have become the main growth engine; oil remains important but has lost relative weight.

targetReport.title: European System of Accounts 2010 (ESA 2010)
targetReport.publisher: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
targetReport.description: The EU's national accounts framework, enacted as Regulation (EU) No 549/2013. Article 1(2) sets out its two parts: 'a methodology (Annex A) on common standards, definitions, classifications and accounting rules that shall be used for compiling accounts and tables on comparable bases for the purposes of the Union' and 'a programme (Annex B) setting out the time limits by which Member States shall transmit to the Commission (Eurostat) the accounts and tables'. Unlike the international standards already in this corpus, ESA 2010 is a Regulation — member states do not adopt it by choice — which is why the EU branch was expected to produce supranational-to-national edges the Canada/US pair lacks. Annex B turned out to name tables and deadlines rather than publications; see the _dropped entries here and in eu-draft-budget.json.
targetReport.cadence_note: A generational standard, revised roughly once every fifteen to twenty years: ESA 1995 preceded it, and a further revision is already anticipated. releases_per_year matches sna-2008 (0.05) so the two read at the same pulse rate; see _open_questions.

release_schedule.note: 2030 is Eurostat's stated aim, not a locked legal date — the ESA 2030 proposal is still in consultation.
